newsitem.title: USA: Record labels seek success with micro-marketing.
newsitem.headline: Record labels seek success with micro-marketing.

text.p: When Virgin Records released the debut album by Britain's Spice Girls in the United States earlier this year, the label knew its worldwide chart-topping feats wouldn't necessarily be repeated here.
Plenty of British artists have had difficulty crossing the Atlantic over the years, whether it be Cliff Richard or Blur, and Virgin, a unit of EMI Group Plc., was taking no chances.

Besides plying the usual marketing avenues such as MTV and VH1, radio, retail, and the media, the label hired a database management firm to conduct a scientific marketing campaign aimed at identifying likely fans on an individual basis.

While database marketing is prevalent in industries from automobiles to health care and packaged goods, the record industry has traditionally opted to plaster its product over the marketplace and see what sticks. The rewards for a lucky few can be huge, but most albums get lost in the shuffle.
Helping make the odds more favourable is Music Marketing Network (MMN), which is 25 percent owned by Illinois-based database management firm Metromail Inc.

Co-founded five years ago by entrepreneur Paul Chachko and former Mercury Records executive John Mazzacco, Red Bank, N.J.-based MMN helps the major labels focus their marketing "I always thought that there was a piston of the engine that was missing," said Chachko, 38, who made his money with a chain of flower stores, "and that was the power of the ultimate buyer, the consumer. In any other industry, the consumer had a lot of motivation to react to promotions and react to product, and word of mouth was huge."

MMN has the names and details of more than 4 million active, entertainment-buying consumers in its database, and the number grows by about 100,000 a month, largely through "bounceback" cards -- reply-paid questionnaires enclosed with CDs and cassettes. Each individual's file has up to 300 additional pieces of information appended by Metromail.

It all sounds very "Big Brother," but the names and addresses are confidential to MMN. Everything else, though, is up for grabs. Later this year, MMN will start selling a desktop delivery system, which will offer consumer profiles on the entertainment business.

"An entertainment marketer could pull up the system, get a profile of a Smashing Pumpkins buyer, either regionally, through age, through sex, through purchasing habits," Chachko said. "You can drill down as far as you want and find out what kind of pets these consumers own ..."
MMN is spending in the low-seven figures to get the intranet-based, password-protected system up and running.

Record labels aren't the only potential customers. Companies such as breweries or automakers, looking to sponsor a tour or advertise in a music publication, for example, will be able to fine-tune their promotions accordingly.

As it turned out, the Spice Girls have become a success in the United States. MTV, radio and news coverage created an initial buzz that saw "Spice" make its debut on the U.S. album charts at No. 6 in February. MMN's challenge was to build a fan base that could sustain the record until the next one comes out.

"Here they come onto the scene this year and literally explode, just do fantastically well," Chachko said. "But yet they don't have a real strong tour to support it, and they're being touted as a video band and a radio band. But there's really no credibility behind it."

The reply rate on the bounceback card sent out with "Spice" has been 10 percent to 12 percent, or about 120,000 fans, well above the standard. The next time the Spice Girls do anything, the fans will receive newsletters or product or discount coupons, ostensibly from the band itself, encouraging them to get out and buy whatever is being promoted.

After 15 weeks of release, "Spice" finally made it to No. 1, and has spent a total of five weeks at the top of the charts, selling about 3 million copies. Since the Spice Girls, or fellow client Alanis Morissette, have crossed over into superstar status, MMN's involvement won't be as crucial on their next albums.
For artists at the next level, such as Rusted Root or Blues Traveller, MMN's database will prove invaluable in driving the other parts of the marketing engine.
